# F3 — SEMANTIC GROUPS TABLE

| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|------------|------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------|
| GROUP 1: Truth-Telling and Speech Acts | Terms and constructions used when describing the act of speaking truthfully or falsely, focusing on the communicative act itself rather than the content's correspondence to reality. These expressions center on what people do when they speak—whether they tell truth or lies—and are commonly used in moral evaluations of speech behavior and in contexts of testimony or reporting. | სიმართლე თქვა (simart'le t'qva) "to tell the truth"; ტყუილი თქვა (ṭq'uili t'qva) "to tell a lie"; სიმართლე ამბობს (simart'le ambobs) "tells the truth" (habitual); ტყუილი ამბობს (ṭq'uili ambobs) "tells lies" (habitual); ჭეშმარიტი სიტყვა თქვა (č'ešmarit'i sit'q'va t'qva) "to speak a true word"; უტყუარი (uṭq'uari) "truthful, honest"; მატყუარა (maṭq'uara) "liar, deceiver"; ტყუილმოთქმელი (ṭq'uilmotxmeli) "liar, one who speaks lies"; გულწრფელად ამბობს (gulc'rpelad ambobs) "speaks sincerely" | გულწრფელი (gulc'rpeli) "sincere, honest" — appears in both Group 1 (Truth-Telling) when characterizing speech acts and Group 11 (Sincerity) when characterizing feelings/persons, bridging communicative honesty and emotional authenticity | Distinguished by focus on the speech act itself. Terms pattern with verbs of speaking (თქვა t'qva "say," ამბობს ambobs "tells") and are used to evaluate speakers' honesty or dishonesty. Common in moral discourse about communication and in legal contexts concerning testimony. |
| GROUP 2: Correctness and Error in Statements | Terms used to evaluate whether statements, answers, or judgments are factually correct or incorrect, without necessarily implying moral evaluation of the speaker. These expressions focus on accuracy of content and are commonly used in educational, technical, and everyday contexts where getting facts right matters, such as answering questions, following instructions, or making accurate assessments. | სწორი (sc'ori) "correct, right"; სწორი პასუხი (sc'ori p'asuxi) "correct answer"; სწორად (sc'orad) "correctly"; სწორად გააკეთა (sc'orad gaak'et'a) "did it correctly"; მცდარი (mcdari) "false, erroneous, mistaken"; მცდარი აზრი (mcdar azri) "wrong opinion"; არასწორი (arasc'ori) "incorrect, wrong"; მართებული (mart'ebuli) "correct, proper, justified"; ზუსტი (zusti) "precise, accurate, exact"; ზუსტი პასუხი (zusti p'asuxi) "precise answer" | მართალი (mart'ali) "right, correct, just" — appears in Group 2 (Correctness) for factual accuracy and Group 7 (Moral Rightness) for ethical evaluation, bridging epistemic and moral domains | Distinguished from Group 1 by focus on factual accuracy rather than speaker honesty. Terms commonly appear in educational contexts (correct/incorrect answers), technical instructions (doing something correctly), and evaluations of accuracy. The term მცდარი specifically implies error or mistake rather than deliberate deception. |
| GROUP 3: Reality and Genuineness | Terms distinguishing what is real, genuine, or authentic from what is fake, counterfeit, or merely apparent. # F4 Construction Table — Yoruba (yo)

| NEGATIVE ATTRIBUTION | Irọ́ kọ́ | Irọ́ kọ́ | It's not a lie | **Kọ́** is extremely common in conversational denials and rebuttals. Often used alone as a one-word denial. | [CORE] |
| ADNOMINAL MODIFICATION | Ọ̀rọ̀ tọ́ | Ọ̀rọ̀ tọ́ | True statement | Direct N+ADJ order is standard and productive. No copula required for attributive modification. | [CORE] |

| CAUSATIVE | Ó mú mi gbàgbọ́ | Ó mú mi gbàgbọ́ | He/She made me believe | **Mú** marks direct causation. Common with psychological verbs in truth domain (cause to believe, know, understand). | [CORE] |

| IMPERATIVE | Má purọ́! | Má purọ́! | Don't lie! | **Má** marks prohibitive. **Má purọ́** is one of the most basic moral commands in Yoruba culture. | [CORE] |
| COMPLEMENTATION | Mo gbàgbọ́ pé ó tọ́ | Mo gbàgbọ́ pé ó tọ́ | I believe that it is true | **Pé** 'that' introduces declarative complements. Standard with epistemic verbs (gbàgbọ́, mọ̀, rò). | [CORE] |

| ADVERBIAL MODIFICATION (MANNER) | Ní òtítọ́ | Ní òtítọ́ | Truthfully, honestly | **Ní òtítọ́** is extremely common as both manner adverbial and discourse marker. Used to emphasize sincerity. | [CORE] |
| ADVERBIAL MODIFICATION (MANNER) | Gbàgbọ́ láì rí | Gbàgbọ́ láì rí | Believe without seeing | **Láì** 'without' plus verb creates negative manner. Common in religious and philosophical discourse. | [CORE] |
| DEGREE MODIFICATION | Ó tọ́ púpọ̀ | Ó tọ́ púpọ̀ | It is very correct/quite true | **Púpọ̀** 'very/much' is the standard intensifier. Follows predicate. Very productive. | [CORE] |

# F5 Opposition Table — Yoruba (yo)

| Term A | Term B | Transliteration | Translation | Contrast Description | Contrast Type | Epistemic Status |

| òtítọ́ | irọ́ | òtítọ́ / irọ́ | truth / lie, falsehood | òtítọ́ refers to statements or representations that correspond to reality, while irọ́ refers to statements known to be false or deliberate misrepresentation. This is the primary lexical opposition in the truth domain. | lexical | [CORE] |
| tọ́ | kò tọ́ | tọ́ / kò tọ́ | to be correct, true / to not be correct, not true | tọ́ affirms the correctness or truth of statements, while kò tọ́ negates it using the standard negative marker kò. This is the basic morphological negation of the stative verb. | morphological | [CORE] |

| olótítọ́ | apurọ́ / ẹlẹ́rọ́ | olótítọ́ / apurọ́, ẹlẹ́rọ́ | truthful person / liar | olótítọ́ characterizes persons who habitually speak truthfully, while apurọ́ and ẹlẹ́rọ́ characterize persons who habitually lie. These are agentive nominalizations expressing opposite character traits. | lexical | [CORE] |

This is morphological negation of the epistemic verb. | morphological | [CORE] |
| agbàgbọ́ | aláìgbàgbọ́ | agbàgbọ́ / aláìgbàgbọ́ | believer / unbeliever, skeptic | agbàgbọ́ characterizes persons who believe, while aláìgbàgbọ́ characterizes persons who lack belief, using the negative possessive prefix oní-àì-. This opposition is particularly common in religious contexts. | morphological | [CORE] |
| dájú | kò dájú | dájú / kò dájú | to be certain, sure / to not be certain, not sure | dájú expresses epistemic certainty, while kò dájú expresses uncertainty or lack of certainty. This is standard morphological negation of the certainty predicate. | morphological | [CORE] |
| òdodo | àìṣe òdodo | òdodo / àìṣe òdodo | righteousness, justice / unrighteousness, injustice | òdodo refers to moral and legal correctness, while àìṣe òdodo (literally "not doing righteousness") refers to violation of moral standards. | ìwà rere | ìwà búburú | ìwà rere / ìwà búburú | good character / bad character | ìwà rere describes virtuous conduct patterns, while ìwà búburú describes immoral conduct patterns. These are fixed compounds using the general evaluative adjectives rere "good" and búburú "bad." | lexical | [CORE] |
| ṣe déédé | àìṣedéédé | ṣe déédé / àìṣedéédé | to do correctly / incorrectness, not doing correctly | ṣe déédé describes accurate execution, while àìṣedéédé refers to failure to meet proper standards, using the negative prefix àì-. This opposition focuses on procedural correctness. | morphological | [CORE] |
| gidi | kì í ṣe gidi | gidi / kì í ṣe gidi | genuine, real / not genuine, not real | gidi affirms authenticity, while kì í ṣe gidi denies it using the emphatic negative copula. This opposition distinguishes genuine instances from fakes or imitations. | morphological | [CORE] |

| GROUP 1: Predicative Truth Evaluation | Expressions used to affirm or deny that a statement, claim, or proposition corresponds to reality. # CLCA Protocol v3.2 — F3 Semantic Groups Table
# Language: Tamil (ta)

| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|------------|------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------|
| GROUP 1: Basic Truth-Falsehood Opposition | This group contains the primary everyday terms used to assert or deny the truth-value of statements, claims, or situations. These terms function as direct opposites in colloquial and formal discourse, appearing in parallel constructions and serving as the default vocabulary for truth-evaluation in everyday speech. | உண்மை (uṇmai) "truth"; பொய் (poy) "falsehood, lie"; உண்மையான (uṇmaiyāṉa) "true, genuine"; பொய்யான (poyyāṉa) "false, fake"; நிஜம் (nijam) "truth, reality" | உண்மையான (uṇmaiyāṉa) also appears in Group 10; பொய்யான (poyyāṉa) also appears in Group 10 | These terms appear in direct opposition (உண்மை vs. பொய்), in parallel verbal constructions (உண்மை சொல் vs. பொய் சொல்), and in interrogative-confirmatory exchanges. They are the most frequent terms in everyday truth-evaluation. |
| GROUP 2: Correctness and Error | This group contains terms used to evaluate the accuracy or appropriateness of statements, actions, calculations, or judgments. # CLCA Protocol v3.4 — F4 Construction Table
# Language: Turkish (tr)

| Construction Type | Example | Transliteration | Translation | Usage Notes | Epistemic Status |
|------------------|---------|-----------------|-------------|-------------|------------------|
| **1. ATTRIBUTION** | Bu doğru | bu doğru | This is true | Extremely common in everyday speech and writing. Zero copula is the unmarked pattern for present tense third person. Used across all registers. | [CORE] |
| **1. ATTRIBUTION** | Söylediğin gerçek değil | söylediğin gerçek değil | What you said is not true/real | Standard negative attribution. No register restrictions. | [CORE] |
| **1. ATTRIBUTION (Alternate)** | Bu doğrudur (with overt copula -dır) | bu doğrudur | This is true | Formal/written register variant. Adds emphatic or authoritative tone. Less common in speech. | [MARGINAL] |
| **2. NEGATIVE ATTRIBUTION** | Bu doğru değil | bu doğru değil | This is not true/correct | The standard and only productive negative copula pattern for present tense. No register or context restrictions. | [CORE] |
| **2. NEGATIVE ATTRIBUTION** | Gerçek değil, yalan | gerçek değil, yalan | It's not true, it's a lie | Common contrastive pattern. Used in argumentative and explanatory contexts. | [CORE] |
| **3. ADNOMINAL MODIFICATION** | doğru bilgi | doğru bilgi | correct information, true information | Highly productive across all noun types. No restrictions on noun class (abstract or concrete). Used in all registers. | [CORE] |
| **3. ADNOMINAL MODIFICATION** | yanlış anlama | yanlış anlama | misunderstanding, wrong understanding | Productive with both concrete and abstract nouns. Common in everyday usage. | [CORE] |
| **4. BECOME / INCHOATIVE** | Gerçeğe dönüştü | gerçeğe dönüştü | It turned into reality | More formal/literary. Emphasizes transformation process. Less common than *çıkmak* pattern. | [MARGINAL] |
| **4. BECOME / INCHOATIVE** | Doğru çıktı | doğru çıktı | It turned out to be true | Very common in everyday speech. Emphasizes revelation or discovery of truth-value. Preferred over *dönüşmek* in colloquial contexts. | [CORE] |
| **5. CAUSATIVE** | Gerçekleştirmek | gerçekleştirmek | to realize, to make real | The only productive morphological causative in truth domain. Common in all registers. Specifically means "bring about, actualize." | [CORE] |
| **5. CAUSATIVE** | Doğru göstermek | doğru göstermek | to show to be true, to demonstrate truth | Light verb construction is preferred over morphological causative for most truth-domain causation. Common in argumentative and evidential contexts. | [CORE] |
| **5. CAUSATIVE (Alternates)** | Doğru kabul etmek, gerçeği ortaya çıkarmak | doğru kabul etmek, gerçeği ortaya çıkarmak | to accept as true, to reveal the truth | Multiple light verb strategies are more productive than morphological causatives. Each has specific semantic nuances. | [CORE] |

# G1 — Cross-Language Summary of Observed Semantic Organization

---

## 1. Language Inventory

- **ka — Georgian**: Agglutinative language with rich derivational morphology; truth vocabulary organized around several distinct roots (mart'l-, č'ešmarit'-, namdvil-, ṭq'uil-) with extensive semantic extension into legal, religious, and administrative domains.
- **yo — Yoruba**: Tonal language with productive nominal and agentive derivation; truth vocabulary centers on tọ́ (straight/correct), òtítọ́ (truth), irọ́ (lie), and òdodo (righteousness), with strong integration of moral and factual evaluation.
- **fi — Finnish**: Agglutinative language with highly productive suffixation; truth vocabulary built around tosi/tode- (true/real), oikea (right/correct), väärä (wrong/false), and valhe (lie), with extensive compound formation and grammaticalized discourse markers.
- **eu — Basque**: Agglutinative language with ergative morphology; truth vocabulary centers on egia (truth), gezur (lie), zuzen (straight/correct), and benetako (real/genuine), with productive relational suffixation and notable gaps in causative and agentive derivation.
- **ta — Tamil**: Agglutinative Dravidian language with two major truth roots (uṇmai, mey) and a primary falsehood root (poy), showing register stratification between colloquial and literary/philosophical usage, with extensive compound formation.
- **id — Indonesian**: Isolating language with productive affixation (meN-, ke-...-an, peN-...-an); truth vocabulary centers on benar (true/correct), salah (wrong), jujur (honest), palsu (fake), and asli (genuine), with extensive light verb constructions.
- **tr — Turkish**: Agglutinative language with productive suffixation; truth vocabulary centers on doğru (true/correct/straight), gerçek (real/genuine), hak (right/truth/due), yanlış (wrong), and sahte (fake), with notable polysemy in hak and doğru.
- **ko — Korean**: Agglutinative language with Sino-Korean and native vocabulary strata; truth vocabulary includes jinsil (truth), geojit (falsehood), sasil (fact), jinjja (real), gajja (fake), and sil- (real/actual) compounds, with strong asymmetry between positive and negative agentive forms.

---

## 2. Per-Language Semantic Sketch

### Georgian (ka)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps:** Georgian maintains several distinct truth-related roots that partially overlap in usage. The mart'l- root covers correctness, moral rightness, and extends into legal/administrative domains (samamart'ali "law," mart'va "management"). The č'ešmarit'i root emphasizes genuineness and authenticity, appearing frequently in religious and elevated discourse. The namdvil- root focuses on ontological reality and authenticity. The ṭq'uil- root covers falsehood and deception. The sando root covers reliability/trustworthiness as a distinct category. Borrowed terms (realuri, obiekṭuri, subiekṭuri, pakṭi) occupy formal/technical registers.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:** The mart'l- root shows exceptional productivity, extending from correctness into management (mart'va), law (samart'ali), orthography (mart'lc'era), and Orthodox Christianity (mart'lmadidebeli). The ṭq'uil- root generates extensive deception vocabulary including reflexive (tviṭmoṭq'ueba "self-deception") and multiple aspectual variants (moṭq'ueba, gaṭq'ueba, šeṭq'ueba). Negative forms use u- prefix (uṭq'uari "truthful," umart'ebulo "incorrect"). Abstract nouns use -oba or -eba suffixes productively.

**Constructional patterns and absences:** Light verb constructions with verbs of speaking (t'qva "say," ambobs "tells") are central. Spatial metaphors for epistemic distance (simart'lestan axlos/shors "close to/far from truth") are attested. Revelation constructions (gamovlinda "was revealed," gamoač'ina "revealed") are productive. No dedicated causative construction for "making true" is identified; the language prefers revelation/verification constructions.

**Oppositional structures:** Primary lexical oppositions: simart'le/ṭq'uili (truth/lie), ṭq'uili/uṭq'uari (liar/truthful), ṭq'uili/namdvili (false/real). Morphological oppositions using u- (negative) and -iani (possessive). Constructional oppositions: salata/paljastua (conceal/reveal), axlos/shors (close/far from truth).

---

### Yoruba (yo)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps:** Yoruba organizes truth vocabulary around tọ́ (to be straight/correct), which covers both factual accuracy and moral rightness. The noun òtítọ́ (truth) derives from this root. Falsehood is covered by irọ́ (lie) and purọ́ (to lie). Moral rightness has a distinct term òdodo (righteousness/justice), which is paired with òtítọ́ in fixed binomials. Belief/trust is covered by gbàgbọ́. Genuineness uses gidi and jẹ́jẹ́. The distinction between factual accuracy and moral rightness is less sharply lexicalized than in some other languages, with tọ́ serving both functions.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:** The -garri suffix (worthy of) productively creates evaluative adjectives: sinesgarria (believable), fidagarria (reliable), zalantzagarria (doubtful). Agentive forms use oní- prefix (olótítọ́ "truthful person," olódodo "righteous person"). Negative agentives use oní-àì- (aláìgbàgbọ́ "unbeliever"). The verbal system uses serial verb constructions productively (sọ...jáde "tell...out" = reveal). Reduplication intensifies (gidi gidi "very genuine," tọ́tọ́ "very correct").

**Constructional patterns and absences:** Serial verb constructions are a distinctive feature (wá...rí "seek...find"). Focus constructions with ni are primary for contrastive emphasis (Òtítọ́ ni mo sọ "It is truth I spoke"). The causative uses mú (Ó mú mi gbàgbọ́ "He made me believe"). No morphological causative for truth-domain terms is identified; light verb constructions dominate.

**Oppositional structures:** Primary lexical oppositions: òtítọ́/irọ́ (truth/lie), tọ́/kò tọ́ (correct/not correct), ìwà rere/ìwà búburú (good character/bad character). Morphological negation uses àì- prefix (àìtọ́ "incorrectness," àìgbàgbọ́ "unbelief"). Scalar oppositions: irọ́ kékeré/irọ́ ńlá (small lie/big lie).

---

### Finnish (fi)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps:** Finnish organizes truth vocabulary around tosi/tode- (true/real), oikea (right/correct/genuine), väärä (wrong/false), and valhe (lie). The tosi root shows extensive polysemy: it covers propositional truth, ontological reality (tosielämä "real life"), and functions as a colloquial intensifier (tosi hyvä "really good"). The oikea root covers correctness, direction (right vs. left), genuineness, and legal rights (oikeus). The väärä root covers factual error, moral wrong, and counterfeit. Borrowed terms (objektiivinen, subjektiivinen) occupy academic registers.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:** The tode- root generates an exceptionally large derivational family including inchoative (toteutua, todellistua), causative (toteuttaa, todellistaa), and verification verbs (todistaa, todentaa, todeta). The -uus/-yys suffix productively creates abstract nouns (totuus, rehellisyys, luotettavuus). The epä- prefix creates systematic negations (epätosi, epärehellinen, epäluotettava). The vale- prefix creates counterfeit compounds (valepassi, valenimi). The tosi- prefix creates reality compounds (tositarina, tosielämä). The -tön privative suffix creates absence adjectives (virheetön "error-free," vilpitön "sincere").

**Constructional patterns and absences:** The fixed expression pitää paikkansa ("holds its place" = is true) is a distinctive idiom. Discourse markers (sebenarnya, totta puhuen) are grammaticalized from truth roots. The language shows a gap: no natural expression for propositions "becoming true" as state change; Finnish prefers revelation/verification constructions (osoittautua todeksi "prove to be true," paljastua "be revealed"). Translative case (-ksi) marks result states in causative constructions (todistaa oikeaksi "prove right," todistaa vääräksi "prove wrong").

**Oppositional structures:** Primary lexical oppositions: tosi/valhe (true/lie), oikea/väärä (right/wrong), aito/väärennös (genuine/forgery). Morphological oppositions using epä- (epätosi, epärehellinen) and -tön (virheetön/virheellinen). Constructional oppositions: pitää paikkansa/ei pidä paikkaansa (is true/is not true), paljastaa/salata (reveal/conceal).

### Basque (eu)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps:** Basque organizes truth vocabulary around egia (truth), gezur (lie), zuzen (straight/correct/direct), and benetako (real/genuine). The zuzen root shows extensive polysemy covering physical straightness, factual correctness, moral rightness, directness (zuzenean "live/directly"), and legal concepts (zuzenbide "law"). The egia root generates a large family of verification and authentication terms. The benetako/itxurazko (real/apparent) opposition covers the reality-appearance distinction. Borrowed terms (faltsua, erreala, fede) are integrated.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:** The -zko/-ezko relational suffix productively creates adjectives (egiazkoa "true," gezurrezko "false"). The -tasun suffix creates abstract nouns (egiazkotasuna, zintzotasuna, zuzentasuna). The -garri suffix creates evaluative adjectives (fidagarria "reliable," sinesgarria "believable," frogagarria "provable"). The -tu verbalizer creates verification verbs (egiazkotu, egiaztatu, ziurtatu). Notable gaps: no productive causative for truth-domain terms (the morphological causative -arazi does not combine with truth roots); no simple verb *gezurtu "to lie" (requires light verb construction gezurra esan). Several positive abstract nominals lack negative counterparts (*gezurtasuna not attested).

**Constructional patterns and absences:** Light verb constructions are obligatory for lying (gezurra esan "tell a lie") and truth-telling (egia esan "tell the truth"). Genitive + postposition constructions are productive (egiaren bila "in search of truth," egiaren alde "on the side of truth"). The -etan locative plural creates idiomatic expressions (gezurretan harrapatu "catch in lies," gezurretan ibili "go about lying"). Causative gap is notable: no productive construction for "making X true."

**Oppositional structures:** Primary lexical oppositions: egia/gezur (truth/lie), egiazkoa/gezurrezko (true/false), zuzena/okerra (correct/wrong), benetako/itxurazko (real/apparent). Morphological oppositions: -garri/-gaitz (worthy of/unable to be: sinesgarria/sinesgaitza). Several expected oppositions are absent or asymmetric: no dedicated lexical opposite for fidagarria (reliable), zintzoa (honest), or egiazkotasuna (truthfulness).

---

### Tamil (ta)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps:** Tamil maintains two major truth roots with register stratification: uṇmai (everyday/formal truth) and mey (literary/philosophical truth/body). The poy root covers falsehood across registers. The cari/tappu pair covers correctness/error in everyday contexts. The nērmai root covers moral honesty/integrity as a distinct category. The sattiyam root (from Sanskrit satya) covers solemn/religious truth. The nijam root (colloquial, borrowed) covers everyday factual truth. The mey root shows systematic polysemy between "truth/reality" and "body/physical," generating a large family of non-truth-domain compounds (meyyeḻuttu "consonant," meycilirppu "goosebumps").

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:** The uṇmai root generates extensive compound vocabulary (uṇmainilai "true state," uṇmaiccāṉṟu "certificate of authenticity," uṇmaivāti "truth-teller"). The poy root generates parallel compounds (poynilai "false state," poyccāṉṟu "false certificate"). Agentive forms show asymmetry: poyyan "liar" (masculine) and poyyāḷ (gender-neutral) exist, but positive agentives use different morphology (uṇmaiyāḷar with honorific suffix). The -āka adverbializer is productive (uṇmaiyāka "truly," poyyāka "falsely," meyyāka "genuinely"). The causative uṇmaippaṭuttu "to verify" uses -paṭuttu, while the falsification causative poyyākku uses -ākku, showing morphological asymmetry.

**Constructional patterns and absences:** Light verb constructions with col (say), pēcu (speak), and kūṟu (state) are central for truth-telling. The existential construction (uṇmai uṇṭu/illai "there is/is no truth") treats truth as a substance that can be present or absent. The discourse marker uṇmaiyil ("in truth, actually") is highly grammaticalized. No productive construction for "making X true" in the sense of causing a proposition to acquire truth value; the language prefers verification/revelation constructions.

**Oppositional structures:** Primary lexical oppositions: uṇmai/poy (truth/falsehood), cari/tappu (correct/wrong), nērmai/kaḷḷam (honesty/deceit). Morphological oppositions: uṇmaiyāka/poyyāka (truthfully/falsely). Asymmetric oppositions: poy kaṇṇīr "crocodile tears" has no positive counterpart; poy nāṭakam "false drama" has no positive counterpart, reflecting a pattern where deceptive/insincere behavior receives lexical marking while genuine behavior is unmarked.

---

### Indonesian (id)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps:** Indonesian organizes truth vocabulary around benar (true/correct), salah (wrong/mistaken), jujur (honest), palsu (fake), and asli (genuine). The benar/salah pair covers factual correctness/error. The jujur/bohong pair covers moral honesty/lying. The palsu/asli pair covers authenticity. The nyata root covers ontological reality. The tepat root covers precision/appropriateness. The sah/valid pair covers legal/formal validity. The salah root shows exceptional productivity in compounds (salah paham "misunderstand," salah sangka "misjudge," salah tulis "typo," salah kaprah "widespread error"), and also grammaticalizes as a quantifier (salah satu "one of").

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:** The meN-...-kan causative is highly productive across truth-domain vocabulary (membenarkan "confirm," menyalahkan "blame," memalsukan "falsify," mengesahkan "validate"). The ke-...-an nominalization creates abstract nouns (kebenaran "truth," kejujuran "honesty," kepalsuan "fakeness"). The peN-...-an nominalization creates process nouns (pembenaran "justification," pemalsuan "forgery"). The se-...-nya pattern creates adverbials (sebenarnya "actually," sejujurnya "honestly," sesungguhnya "truly"). Reduplication intensifies (benar-benar "really," sungguh-sungguh "earnestly"). The salah root grammaticalizes into a quantifier (salah satu "one of"), losing truth-domain semantics entirely.

**Constructional patterns and absences:** Zero copula is the unmarked present-tense predication pattern. The ternyata construction (ter- + nyata) is a grammaticalized evidential marker ("it turns out"). The menjadi construction is the standard inchoative (menjadi kenyataan "become reality"). Authenticity is treated as binary rather than gradable; no natural expression for "becoming more genuine" is attested. The kurang construction creates hedged negations (kurang benar "not quite correct") as a face-saving strategy.

**Oppositional structures:** Primary lexical oppositions: benar/salah (true/wrong), asli/palsu (genuine/fake), jujur/bohong (honest/lying). Morphological oppositions using tidak (tidak benar, tidak jujur) and epä- equivalent. Constructional oppositions: benar atau salah (true or false), asli atau palsu (genuine or fake). Several expected oppositions are absent: sejati (genuine) and hakiki (essential) lack dedicated antonyms.

---

### Turkish (tr)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps:** Turkish organizes truth vocabulary around doğru (true/correct/straight/direct), gerçek (real/genuine), hak (right/truth/due/God), yanlış (wrong/false), and sahte (fake). The doğru root shows extensive polysemy covering propositional truth, physical direction, moral rightness, and directness (doğrudan "directly"). The hak root (from Arabic ḥaqq) covers truth, rights, deservingness, and divine names (Hak Teala "God Almighty"), showing the broadest semantic range of any single root. The gerçek root covers ontological reality and genuineness. Borrowed terms from Arabic (hakikat, sahih, meşru) and Persian (sahte) occupy formal and specialized registers.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:** The -leş- inchoative suffix combines with truth roots (gerçekleşmek "come true," kesinleşmek "become definite"). The -leştir- causative extends this (gerçekleştirmek "realize/implement," kesinleştirmek "finalize"). The -lık/-lik suffix creates abstract nouns (doğruluk "truth/honesty," gerçeklik "reality," haklılık "rightness"). The -la- denominative creates verification verbs (doğrulamak "verify," yanlışlamak "falsify"). The hak root generates an unusually large family of fixed expressions (hak etmek "deserve," hak vermek "agree with," hak yemek "violate rights," hakkında "about/concerning"). The çıkmak construction (doğru çıkmak "turn out to be true," yanlış çıkmak "turn out to be wrong") is the preferred inchoative pattern for truth-domain terms.

**Constructional patterns and absences:** The çıkmak construction is the primary inchoative for truth revelation (doğru çıkmak, haklı çıkmak). Light verb constructions with etmek, olmak, vermek, and söylemek are central. The postposition hakkında (from hak) is fully grammaticalized for "about/concerning." Alliterative fixed collocations are productive (doğru dürüst, doğru düzgün, yalan dolan). The conditional -sa/-se vs. counterfactual -saydı distinction marks open vs. contrary-to-fact conditions.

**Oppositional structures:** Primary lexical oppositions: doğru/yanlış (true/wrong), gerçek/sahte (real/fake), haklı/haksız (right/unjust). Morphological oppositions using -sız privative (haksız, tutarsız, geçersiz, uygunsuz). The -lı possessive vs. -sız privative pair is highly productive. Constructional oppositions: doğru çıkmak/yanlış çıkmak (turn out true/false), gerçeği söylemek/gerçeği gizlemek (tell/hide truth).

---

### Korean (ko)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps:** Korean maintains a Sino-Korean/native vocabulary distinction in the truth domain. Sino-Korean terms (jinsil "truth," sasil "fact," jinjeong "genuine," jeongjik "honest") occupy formal registers, while native terms (jinjja "real," gajja "fake," matda "correct," teullida "wrong") are colloquial. The sil- (實) prefix generates a large family of "actual/real" compounds (silje "reality," silche "substance," siljil "essence," sillyeok "actual ability," siljeok "actual results"). The jin- (眞) prefix generates authenticity compounds (jinsim "sincere heart," jinui "true intention," jinga "true value," jinmyeonmok "true character"). The geojit root covers falsehood and generates extensive compounds (geojinmal "lie," geojitjeungeon "false testimony," geojitjeongbo "false information").

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:** The -seong suffix creates abstract quality nouns (jinsilseong "truthfulness," sinbingseong "credibility," jinjeongseonng "authenticity"). Agentive forms show strong asymmetry: geojinmaljaengi "liar" is a productive agentive, but no corresponding positive agentive (*jinsiljaengi "truth-teller") is attested. The -투성이 suffix creates saturation expressions (geojittuseongi "full of lies") with no positive counterpart. The -배기 suffix creates emphatic forms (jinjjabaegi "the real deal," gajjabaegi "total fake"). The sil- compounds show a gap: failure terms (silpae "failure," silsu "mistake," silmang "disappointment") use the same sil- root but fall outside the truth-evaluation domain.

**Constructional patterns and absences:** Light verb constructions with malhada (say), balkhida (reveal), sumgida (hide), and hwaginhada (confirm) are central. The balkhyeojida/deureonada (be revealed/emerge) constructions are the primary patterns for truth revelation. Agentive nominalization is strongly asymmetric: the language marks habitual liars but not habitual truth-tellers. The discourse marker sasireun ("in fact, actually") is highly grammaticalized. No productive causative for "making X true" is identified.

**Oppositional structures:** Primary lexical oppositions: jinsil/geojit (truth/falsehood), jinjja/gajja (real/fake), matda/teullida (correct/wrong). Constructional oppositions: jinsireul balkhida/jinsireul sumgida (reveal/hide truth), jinsireul malhada/geojinmareul hada (tell truth/tell lie). Asymmetric oppositions: geojiseobsi "without lies" has no positive counterpart; geojittuseongi "full of lies" has no positive counterpart.

## 3. Cross-Language Summary

### Recurring Convergences (patterns observed across many languages)

- **Straight/direct as a source domain for truth and correctness.** In Yoruba (tọ́ "straight"), Basque (zuzen "straight/correct"), Turkish (doğru "straight/correct/direct"), and Georgian (sc'ori "straight/correct"), the same physical concept of straightness or directness underlies terms for factual correctness and moral rightness. Finnish (oikea "right") and Indonesian (benar, from a root associated with correctness) show related patterns. This is one of the most widely distributed structural features in the data.

- **Separation of factual accuracy from moral honesty.** All eight languages maintain some distinction between terms for factual truth/correctness and terms for moral honesty/integrity, though the degree of lexical separation varies. Georgian distinguishes č'ešmarit'i (true/genuine) from uṭq'uari (truthful/honest). Yoruba distinguishes òtítọ́ (truth) from òdodo (righteousness). Finnish distinguishes tosi (true) from rehellinen (honest). Basque distinguishes egia (truth) from zintzo (honest). Tamil distinguishes uṇmai (truth) from nērmai (honesty). Indonesian distinguishes benar (correct) from jujur (honest). Turkish distinguishes doğru (correct) from dürüst (honest). Korean distinguishes jinsil (truth) from jeongjik (honest). In all cases, the moral honesty term focuses on character and habitual conduct rather than propositional accuracy.

- **Authenticity/genuineness as a distinct semantic area from propositional truth.** All languages maintain vocabulary for distinguishing genuine from fake objects, identities, or representations, typically using different terms from those used for propositional truth. Georgian uses namdvili (real/genuine) vs. q'albi (fake). Yoruba uses gidi (genuine) vs. irọ́ ìṣe (deceptive action). Finnish uses aito (genuine) vs. väärennös (forgery). Basque uses benetako (real) vs. faltsua (fake). Tamil uses acal (genuine) vs. poy (fake). Indonesian uses asli (genuine) vs. palsu (fake). Turkish uses gerçek/asıl (real/original) vs. sahte (fake). Korean uses jinjja (real) vs. gajja (fake).

- **Light verb constructions as the primary pattern for truth-related speech acts.** Across all languages, the act of telling the truth or lying is expressed through light verb constructions combining a truth/falsehood noun with a speech verb, rather than through a single dedicated verb. Georgian: simart'le t'qva (truth + say). Yoruba: sọ òtítọ́ (say + truth), pa irọ́ (do + lie). Finnish: puhua totuutta (speak + truth), puhua valhetta (speak + lie). Basque: egia esan (truth + say), gezurra esan (lie + say). Tamil: uṇmai col (truth + say), poy col (lie + say). Indonesian: mengatakan kebenaran (say + truth). Turkish: doğruyu söylemek (truth + say), yalan söylemek (lie + say). Korean: jinsireul malhada (truth + say), geojinmareul hada (lie + do).

- **Revelation and concealment as a productive constructional pair.** All languages show productive constructions for truth being revealed or hidden, typically using different verbs with the same truth noun. Georgian: gamovlinda (was revealed) vs. damala (hid). Yoruba: fi òtítọ́ hàn (show truth) vs. ṣe àṣírí (keep secret). Finnish: paljastaa totuus (reveal truth) vs. salata totuus (conceal truth). Basque: egia atera (bring out truth) vs. egia ezkutatu (hide truth). Tamil: uṇmai veḷippaṭu (truth comes out) vs. uṇmaiyai maṟai (hide truth). Indonesian: mengungkap kebenaran (reveal truth) vs. menyembunyikan kebenaran (hide truth). Turkish: gerçeği ortaya çıkarmak (bring truth to light) vs. gerçeği gizlemek (hide truth). Korean: jinsireul balkhida (reveal truth) vs. jinsireul sumgida (hide truth).

- **Absence of productive causative constructions for "making X true."** Across all eight languages, no productive morphological or light verb causative construction for causing a proposition to acquire truth value is identified. All languages prefer constructions involving verification, revelation, or confirmation (establishing that something is true) rather than causation of truth. This gap is explicitly noted in Georgian, Basque, Finnish, Tamil, and Indonesian data, and is consistent across the remaining languages.

- **Discourse markers grammaticalized from truth roots.** All languages show at least one highly frequent discourse marker derived from a truth root that introduces corrections, clarifications, or frank statements. Georgian: mart'la (really, colloquial). Yoruba: ní òtítọ́ (in truth). Finnish: sebenarnya (actually), totta puhuen (truthfully speaking). Basque: egia esan (truth be told), benetan (really). Tamil: uṇmaiyil (in truth, actually). Indonesian: sebenarnya (actually), sejujurnya (honestly). Turkish: doğrusu (to tell the truth), aslında (actually). Korean: sasireun (in fact, actually).

---

### Major Divergences (patterns observed in few or one language)

- **Exceptional root polysemy spanning truth, rights, and divine names.** Turkish hak (from Arabic ḥaqq) uniquely covers truth, moral rightness, legal rights, deservingness, and divine names (Hak Teala "God Almighty") within a single root. This breadth of polysemy is not matched by any single root in the other seven languages. The hak root generates fixed expressions spanning moral (hak etmek "deserve"), legal (hak sahibi "rights holder"), interpersonal (hak vermek "agree with"), and religious (hakkın rahmetine kavuşmak "to die") domains.

- **Systematic register stratification between two parallel truth roots.** Tamil uniquely maintains two parallel truth roots (uṇmai and mey) with systematic register stratification: uṇmai is the everyday/formal term while mey is literary/philosophical. Both generate parallel derivational families (uṇmaiyāka/meyyāka "truly," uṇmaiyaṟivu/meyyaṟivu "true knowledge"). No other language in the dataset shows this degree of systematic register-based doubling of a core truth root.

- **Grammaticalization of a truth root into a directional/spatial postposition.** Turkish doğru functions as a postposition meaning "toward" (eve doğru "toward home"), and Georgian mart'l- extends into management/governance (mart'va "management," mart'avs "manages"). While several languages show truth roots extending into spatial/directional domains (Yoruba tọ́ "straight," Basque zuzen "direct"), Turkish shows the most complete grammaticalization of a truth root into a postpositional function.

- **Extensive semantic extension of a truth root into administrative and organizational domains.** Georgian mart'l- uniquely extends into management (mart'va "management," mart'uli "managed"), governance (mart'avs "governs"), and organizational contexts (gamamart'uli "well-organized event"). This administrative extension of a truth/correctness root is not matched in the other languages.

- **Productive tosi- and vale- compound prefixes for reality vs. counterfeit.** Finnish uniquely shows two productive compound-forming prefixes derived from truth roots: tosi- (marking factual/authentic: tositarina "true story," tosielämä "real life," tosi-tv "reality TV") and vale- (marking counterfeit/false: valepassi "fake passport," valenimi "pseudonym"). While other languages form similar compounds, Finnish shows the most systematic and productive use of these prefixes.

- **Exceptional productivity of the salah root in Indonesian.** Indonesian salah (wrong) shows unusual productivity in forming compounds for specific error types (salah paham "misunderstand," salah sangka "misjudge," salah tafsir "misinterpret," salah ucap "slip of tongue," salah tulis "typo," salah hitung "miscalculation," salah lihat "see wrongly," salah dengar "mishear," salah langkah "wrong move," salah jalan "wrong path," salah alamat "wrong address," salah urus "mismanagement," salah guna "misuse"). Additionally, salah grammaticalizes as a quantifier (salah satu "one of"), losing truth-domain semantics entirely. This combination of domain-specific compound productivity and grammaticalization is not matched in other languages.

- **Systematic sil- (實) compound family for actual vs. nominal status.** Korean uniquely shows a large productive family of sil- (實) compounds distinguishing actual from nominal status across multiple domains: sillyeok (actual ability), siljeok (actual results), silhyo (actual effect), silje (actual reality), silche (actual substance), siljil (actual quality), silcheon (actual practice), silhaeng (actual execution), silhyeon (actual realization), silmul (actual object), silgam (sense of reality). While other languages have terms for this distinction, Korean shows the most systematic and productive compound family for it.

---

### Asymmetries, Gaps, and Irregularities

- **Asymmetric agentive nominalization: liars are marked, truth-tellers are not.** Across multiple languages, agentive forms for habitual liars are more lexicalized and productive than corresponding forms for habitual truth-tellers. Georgian: maṭq'uara "liar" (productive) vs. no standard agentive for "truth-teller." Yoruba: apurọ́ "liar" (productive) vs. olótítọ́ "truthful person" (less common). Finnish: no dedicated agentive for either, but negative character is more marked. Basque: gezurtia "liar" (productive) vs. egiazale "truth-lover" (less common, different morphology). Tamil: poyyan "liar" (masculine agentive) vs. uṇmaiyāḷar "truthful person" (honorific, different suffix). Indonesian: pembohong "liar" (productive) vs. no standard agentive for "truth-teller." Turkish: yalancı "liar" (lexicalized) vs. no standard agentive for "truth-teller." Korean: geojinmaljaengi "liar" (productive) vs. no attested *jinsiljaengi. This asymmetry is consistent across all eight languages.

- **Asymmetric abstract nominalization: negative abstract nouns are less productive than positive ones.** Several languages show gaps where positive abstract nouns (truthfulness, honesty) are well-attested but corresponding negative abstract nouns (falseness, dishonesty) are less productive or unattested. Basque: egiazkotasuna "truthfulness" is attested but *gezurtasuna "falseness" is not. Finnish: totuus "truth" is highly productive but no direct abstract nominal for "falseness" parallels it. Korean: jinsilseong "truthfulness" is productive but negative counterparts are less systematic. This pattern is less consistent than the agentive asymmetry but appears in multiple languages.

- **Asymmetric privative constructions: absence of falsehood is marked, absence of truth is not.** Several languages show productive constructions for "without lies/falsehood" but no corresponding construction for "without truth." Georgian: uṭq'uari "without lie" (truthful) is productive. Basque: gezurrezko "false" is productive but no *egiazko-gabe "without truth." Korean: geojiseobsi "without lies" is attested but *jinsilseobsi "without truth" is not. Indonesian: tanpa kebohongan "without lies" is possible but tanpa kebenaran "without truth" is less natural. This asymmetry reflects a pattern where deceptive behavior is marked as an absence of something expected, while truthful behavior is the unmarked default.

- **Grammaticalization of truth roots into non-truth domains.** Several languages show truth roots extending into domains with no clear truth-evaluation function. Finnish tosi- extends into intensification (tosi hyvä "really good") and entertainment genres (tosi-tv "reality TV"). Georgian mart'l- extends into management and governance. Turkish doğru extends into spatial direction (postposition "toward"). Korean sil- extends into failure (silpae "failure," silsu "mistake," silmang "disappointment") and spatial terms (silnae "indoor," siloe "outdoor"). Tamil mey extends into body/physical domain (meyyeḻuttu "consonant," meycilirppu "goosebumps"). These extensions are language-specific and do not form a cross-linguistic pattern.

- **The reality-appearance distinction is lexicalized differently across languages.** While all languages distinguish actual reality from mere appearance, the lexical resources differ substantially. Finnish uses todellinen/näennäinen (real/apparent). Basque uses benetako/itxurazko (real/apparent). Turkish uses gerçek/görünür (real/apparent) and aslında (actually). Indonesian uses nyata/semu (real/apparent) and sebenarnya (actually). Korean uses silje/gyeommo (reality/appearance) and sasireun (actually). Georgian uses namdvili/itxurazko (real/apparent). The grammaticalized discourse markers (sebenarnya, aslında, sasireun, etc.) all derive from truth/reality roots and serve to introduce corrections of apparent vs. actual states, but the specific morphological paths differ.

- **Scalar and gradable truth expressions are rare and marginal across languages.** All languages treat core truth terms (true/false, real/fake) as categorical rather than gradable. Scalar expressions (half-true, more true, very true) are attested but marked as marginal or unusual in multiple languages. Georgian: setengah benar "half true" is noted. Finnish: explicitly notes that truth is treated as binary. Basque: egia-maila "truth-level" is marked as marginal. Korean: explicitly notes that truth-domain terms rarely appear in degree comparisons. Indonesian: setengah benar "half true" is attested but marked. This cross-linguistic tendency to treat truth as categorical rather than scalar is one of the most consistent patterns in the data.

- **Verification and authentication vocabulary is more elaborated than falsification vocabulary.** Across languages, the vocabulary for establishing, confirming, or verifying truth tends to be more morphologically elaborated than the vocabulary for creating or establishing falsehood. Georgian: extensive verification vocabulary (damoc'meba, daadast'ura, egiazkotu) vs. limited falsification vocabulary. Finnish: extensive verification family (todistaa, todentaa, todeta, todistus, todistaja, todistustaakka) vs. limited falsification vocabulary. Basque: extensive verification vocabulary (egiazkotu, egiaztatu, frogatu, ziurtatu) vs. no productive *gezurtu. Tamil: uṇmaippaṭuttu "verify" vs. poyyākku "falsify" (marked as less common). This asymmetry may reflect the institutional contexts (legal, administrative, scientific) that drive elaboration of verification vocabulary.

## Narrative Analysis

### Recurring Partition Patterns

**The factual/moral split is present in all eight languages but realized differently.** Every language in the dataset maintains some distinction between terms for propositional truth (whether a statement corresponds to facts) and terms for moral honesty (whether a person is characterized by truthfulness as a virtue). However, the degree of lexical separation varies considerably. Finnish and Indonesian show the clearest separation, with distinct root families for each domain (tosi/totuus vs. rehellinen/vilpitön in Finnish; benar vs. jujur in Indonesian). Yoruba and Georgian show partial merger: Yoruba's tọ́ covers both factual correctness and moral rightness, while Georgian's mart'ali spans both epistemic and moral evaluation. Turkish doğru similarly covers both domains. This suggests that while the factual/moral distinction is universally present, it is not universally lexicalized as a sharp boundary.

**The propositional truth / ontological reality distinction is present but variably lexicalized.** All languages distinguish in some way between "this statement is true" and "this thing is real/genuine," but the lexical resources differ. Finnish maintains the clearest separation (tosi for propositional truth, todellinen for ontological reality, aito for material authenticity). Georgian similarly separates č'ešmarit'i (propositional truth) from namdvili (ontological reality). Indonesian separates benar (propositional correctness) from nyata (ontological reality) and asli (material authenticity). By contrast, Turkish gerçek covers both propositional truth and ontological reality without a sharp lexical boundary, and Korean jinsil similarly spans both. Yoruba gidi covers material genuineness but the propositional/ontological distinction is less sharply marked.

**Correctness and error form a distinct grouping in all languages, but the boundary with propositional truth varies.** All languages have terms for correctness/error that are used in educational, procedural, and evaluative contexts (Georgian sc'ori/mcdari, Yoruba tọ́/àṣìṣe, Finnish oikea/virhe, Basque zuzena/okerra, Tamil cari/tappu, Indonesian benar/salah, Turkish doğru/yanlış, Korean matda/teullida). In most languages, these terms overlap substantially with propositional truth terms—the same word that means "correct" also means "true." The clearest separation is in Tamil, where cari/tappu (colloquial correctness/error) is distinct from uṇmai/poy (truth/falsehood), and in Yoruba, where àṣìṣe (error/mistake) is distinct from irọ́ (lie/falsehood). In other languages (Georgian, Finnish, Indonesian, Turkish, Korean), the correctness and propositional truth groupings share vocabulary or overlap substantially.

**Authenticity/genuineness of objects is universally present but variably integrated with propositional truth.** All eight languages have vocabulary for distinguishing genuine from fake objects, documents, or goods. In Finnish, Basque, Indonesian, and Korean, this grouping is relatively distinct from propositional truth vocabulary (Finnish aito/väärennös, Basque benetako/faltsua, Indonesian asli/palsu, Korean jinjja/gajja). In Georgian, Tamil, and Turkish, the same terms used for propositional truth also cover object authenticity (Georgian namdvili, Tamil uṇmaiyāna, Turkish gerçek/asıl). This suggests that the authenticity grouping is sometimes integrated with propositional truth and sometimes separated from it.

**Reliability/trustworthiness is present as a distinct grouping in most languages.** Georgian (sando), Yoruba (fidagarria via borrowing), Finnish (luotettava, uskottava), Basque (fidagarria, sinesgarria), Tamil (nampakam), Indonesian (dapat dipercaya), Turkish (güvenilir), and Korean (sinbingseong) all maintain vocabulary for evaluating whether sources, persons, or information can be trusted. This grouping is consistently distinct from propositional truth evaluation: reliability concerns whether something will consistently provide accurate information, not whether a specific statement is true. The grouping is present in all eight languages but is more elaborated in some (Finnish, Basque) than others (Yoruba, Tamil).

**Legal/formal validity is present in most languages as a distinct grouping.** Georgian (samart'ali, damoc'meba), Finnish (sah via mengesahkan), Basque (zuzenbide), Tamil (sattiyam in oath contexts), Indonesian (sah, valid), Turkish (geçerli, meşru), and Korean (jinsul, jinwi) all maintain vocabulary for legal or formal validity that is distinct from everyday propositional truth. Yoruba shows this grouping less clearly, with ìdájọ́ (judgment/verdict) and ẹ̀rí (testimony/evidence) covering related functions. The legal/formal validity grouping consistently involves conformity to procedural or institutional requirements rather than correspondence to facts.

### Where Languages Split More Finely

**Finnish shows the most fine-grained partition.** Finnish maintains distinct groupings for propositional truth (tosi/totuus), ontological reality (todellinen/todellisuus), material authenticity (aito/väärennös), deliberate falsehood (valhe/valehdella), moral honesty (rehellinen/vilpitön), reliability (luotettava/uskottava), legal validity (sah via mengesahkan), precision (tepat via ketepatan), and probability (todennäköinen). No other language in the dataset maintains this many distinct groupings with dedicated vocabulary for each. Finnish also uniquely separates sincerity (vilpitön "without deceit") from honesty (rehellinen "honest"), a distinction that is merged in most other languages.

**Korean shows the most elaborate partition of actual vs. nominal status.** The sil- (實) compound family in Korean creates a systematic distinction between actual and nominal status across multiple domains (sillyeok "actual ability" vs. claimed ability, siljeok "actual results" vs. planned results, silhyo "actual effect" vs. intended effect, silje "actual reality" vs. theoretical status). No other language shows this degree of systematic lexical elaboration for the actual/nominal distinction. This grouping is distinct from propositional truth evaluation and from ontological reality, focusing specifically on whether something has real-world impact or is merely formal.

**Basque shows the most elaborate partition of certainty and doubt.** Basque maintains distinct vocabulary for certainty (ziurra, ziurtasuna), doubt (zalantza, zalantzagarria), reliability (fidagarria), and plausibility (sinesgarria) as separate groupings. The -garri suffix productively creates evaluative adjectives for each epistemic stance. Most other languages merge some of these distinctions: Turkish kesin covers both certainty and definiteness; Korean hwaksilhada covers both certainty and reliability; Indonesian tidak yakin covers uncertainty without distinguishing doubt from unreliability.

**Tamil shows the most elaborate partition by register.** Tamil uniquely maintains two parallel truth roots (uṇmai and mey) with systematic register stratification, effectively creating two versions of the propositional truth grouping differentiated by formality and philosophical depth. Additionally, Tamil maintains a distinct solemn/religious truth grouping (sattiyam) that is separate from both everyday and literary truth. No other language shows this three-way register partition within the truth domain.

### Where Languages Merge Distinctions

**Turkish hak merges truth, rights, deservingness, and divine names.** The Turkish hak root (from Arabic ḥaqq) uniquely merges what other languages treat as distinct groupings: propositional truth (hak "truth"), moral rightness (haklı "right/justified"), legal rights (hak sahibi "rights holder"), deservingness (hak etmek "to deserve"), and divine names (Hak Teala "God Almighty"). In all other languages, these functions are distributed across separate roots. The merger in Turkish appears to reflect the Arabic source word's semantic breadth rather than a Turkish-specific innovation.

**Yoruba tọ́ merges factual correctness and moral rightness more completely than other languages.** While most languages show some overlap between correctness and moral rightness, Yoruba tọ́ covers both domains without a clear lexical boundary. The same verb that means "to be correct" (ó tọ́ "it is correct") also means "to be morally right" (kì í tọ́ láti ṣe bẹ́ẹ̀ "it is not right to do that"). Other languages that show this merger (Georgian mart'ali, Turkish doğru) maintain additional terms that more clearly separate the domains, but Yoruba shows the most complete merger.

**Indonesian salah merges factual error, moral wrong, and quantification.** Indonesian salah covers factual incorrectness (salah jawaban "wrong answer"), moral transgression (salah besar "grave wrong"), and grammaticalizes as a quantifier (salah satu "one of"). The quantifier use is entirely outside the truth domain and represents a complete semantic shift. No other language in the dataset shows a truth-domain term grammaticalizing into a quantifier.

**Georgian mart'l- merges correctness, moral rightness, management, and religious identity.** The Georgian mart'l- root covers factual correctness (mart'ali "correct"), moral rightness (mart'ali "righteous"), management/governance (mart'va "management," mart'avs "governs"), and religious identity (mart'lmadidebeli "Orthodox Christian"). The management and religious extensions are not found in other languages and represent a distinctive merger of the correctness domain with administrative and confessional domains.

### Cases Where a Language Lacks a Clear Contrast Found Elsewhere

**No language lacks the truth/falsehood distinction, but the lexical realization varies.** All eight languages maintain some lexical contrast between truth and falsehood. However, the degree to which this contrast is lexically elaborated differs substantially. Finnish and Korean show the most elaborate falsehood vocabulary (Finnish: valhe, valehdella, vale- prefix, harhaanjohtava, petollinen; Korean: geojit, geojinmal, geojitjeungeon, geojitjeongbo, geojittuseongi). Yoruba and Basque show somewhat less elaborate falsehood vocabulary, though both maintain productive systems.

**Plausibility/seeming-true is present in some languages but absent or marginal in others.** Finnish (uskottava "believable," todennäköinen "probable"), Turkish (makul "reasonable," akla yakın "plausible"), and Korean (geureoldeuthada "plausible") maintain dedicated vocabulary for the epistemic category of seeming-true or being plausible. Yoruba, Basque, and Tamil show this category less clearly in the data. Georgian and Indonesian have some relevant vocabulary (Georgian: sinesgarria via borrowing; Indonesian: masuk akal "makes sense") but it is less elaborated. This suggests that plausibility as a distinct epistemic category is present in some languages but not universally lexicalized.

**Moral righteousness as a distinct grouping is present in Yoruba and Georgian but less clear in others.** Yoruba òdodo (righteousness/justice) and Georgian samart'liani (just/fair) maintain a distinct grouping for moral righteousness that goes beyond simple honesty to cover justice, fairness, and conformity to moral law. Finnish, Basque, and Indonesian show this category less clearly, with honesty terms (rehellinen, zintzo, jujur) covering the moral domain without a separate righteousness grouping. Tamil niyāyam (justice/fairness) and Korean jeongdanghada (legitimate/justified) cover related territory but are less central to the truth domain.

**Testimony/evidence as a distinct grouping is present in some languages but absent in others.** Yoruba (ẹ̀rí "witness/testimony," jẹ́rìí "to testify"), Finnish (todistaja "witness," todistus "testimony/certificate," todistustaakka "burden of proof"), and Korean (jinsul "statement/testimony," jinwi "truth or falsehood") maintain dedicated vocabulary for testimony and evidence as distinct from general truth-evaluation. Georgian (damoc'meba "verification/attestation"), Basque (lekukotza "testimony"), and Tamil (sāṭci "witness/testimony") show related vocabulary. Indonesian and Turkish show this category less clearly in the data, with verification vocabulary (membenarkan, doğrulamak) covering related functions without a dedicated testimony grouping.

**Consistency/coherence as a distinct grouping is present in Turkish and Finnish but absent or marginal in others.** Turkish tutarlı/tutarsız (consistent/inconsistent) and Finnish johdonmukainen (consistent) maintain a distinct grouping for logical consistency or coherence of arguments and behavior. This grouping is not clearly present in Yoruba, Basque, Tamil, or Korean data. Georgian and Indonesian show some related vocabulary but it is not elaborated as a distinct grouping. This suggests that consistency/coherence is a language-specific elaboration rather than a universal partition.

### Well-Attested Cross-Language Patterns vs. Single-Language Observations

**Well-attested across all or most languages:**
- The truth/falsehood lexical opposition (all eight languages)
- The factual/moral honesty distinction (all eight languages, variably realized)
- Light verb constructions for truth-telling and lying (all eight languages)
- Revelation/concealment as a productive constructional pair (all eight languages)
- Asymmetric agentive nominalization (liars marked, truth-tellers unmarked) (all eight languages)
- Absence of productive causative for "making X true" (all eight languages)
- Discourse markers grammaticalized from truth roots (all eight languages)
- Authenticity/genuineness as a distinct grouping (all eight languages)
- Reliability/trustworthiness as a distinct grouping (all eight languages)
- Categorical rather than scalar treatment of core truth terms (all eight languages)

**Attested in several but not all languages:**
- Legal/formal validity as a distinct grouping (six of eight languages clearly; Yoruba and Tamil less clearly)
- Plausibility/seeming-true as a distinct grouping (Finnish, Turkish, Korean clearly; others less so)
- Precision/exactness as a distinct grouping (Finnish, Georgian, Tamil, Indonesian clearly; others less so)
- Testimony/evidence as a distinct grouping (Yoruba, Finnish, Korean clearly; others less so)
- Certainty/doubt as a distinct grouping (Basque, Turkish, Korean clearly; others less so)

# G3 — Emergent Cross-Language Semantic Dimensions

## 1. Methodology and Scope

The dimensions below are inferred directly from the F3 semantic grouping tables and supporting F1–F2 evidence across all eight languages. Each dimension is defined by patterns of co-occurrence, lexical opposition, derivational clustering, and constructional parallelism visible in the data. No dimension is proposed unless it is supported by evidence from at least two languages; single-language observations are noted as such. Dimensions are ordered from most to least cross-linguistically robust.

---

## 2. Proposed Dimensions

---

### DIMENSION A: Propositional Correspondence

**Definition.** This dimension covers the evaluation of whether a statement, claim, or piece of information corresponds to actual states of affairs. Terms in this dimension are used when the question is whether what is said or represented matches what is the case. It is the most basic truth-evaluation dimension and is present in all eight languages.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: simart'le (truth), č'ešmarit'i (true), ṭq'uili (lie), mcdari (erroneous)
- Yoruba: òtítọ́ (truth), tọ́ (to be correct/true), irọ́ (lie/falsehood)
- Finnish: tosi (true), totuus (truth), valhe (lie), epätosi (untrue)
- Basque: egia (truth), egiazkoa (true), gezurra (lie), gezurrezko (false)
- Tamil: uṇmai (truth), poy (falsehood), uṇmaiyāna (true), poyyāna (false)
- Indonesian: benar (true/correct), kebenaran (truth), bohong (lie), kebohongan (falsehood)
- Turkish: doğru (true/correct), doğruluk (truth/correctness), yanlış (wrong/false), yalan (lie)
- Korean: jinsil (truth), sasil (fact), geojit (falsehood), geojinmal (lie)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. In all languages this dimension generates the primary lexical opposition (truth term vs. falsehood term) and the primary light verb constructions for truth-telling and lying. The dimension is categorical rather than scalar in all languages: core truth terms resist degree modification.

---

### DIMENSION B: Moral Honesty / Integrity of Character

**Definition.** This dimension covers the evaluation of persons or conduct as characterized by truthfulness, integrity, and absence of deception as a habitual or dispositional quality. Terms in this dimension evaluate character and communicative ethics rather than the truth-value of specific propositions. The focus is on the speaker or agent rather than on the content of statements.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: uṭq'uari (truthful, honest, infallible), uṭq'uaroba (truthfulness), gulsindeli (sincere)
- Yoruba: olótítọ́ (truthful person), ìwà rere (good character), òdodo ọkàn (uprightness of heart)
- Finnish: rehellinen (honest), rehellisyys (honesty), vilpitön (sincere, without deceit), vilpittömyys (sincerity)
- Basque: zintzo/zintzoa (honest, sincere), zintzotasuna (honesty), zintzoki (honestly)
- Tamil: nērmai (honesty, integrity), nērmaiyāna (honest), kaḷḷam (deceit, as negative pole)
- Indonesian: jujur (honest), kejujuran (honesty), sejujurnya (honestly speaking)
- Turkish: dürüst (honest), dürüstlük (honesty), samimi (sincere), içten (heartfelt)
- Korean: jeongjik (honest), jeongjikada (to be honest), soljik (frank), soljikada (to be frank)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. In all languages this dimension is distinct from Dimension A: the moral honesty terms evaluate persons and habitual conduct, while propositional truth terms evaluate specific statements. The degree of lexical separation varies: Finnish and Indonesian show the clearest separation; Yoruba tọ́ and Turkish doğru partially merge this dimension with Dimension A. Agentive nominalization is asymmetric in all languages: terms for habitual liars are more productive than terms for habitual truth-tellers.

---

### DIMENSION C: Ontological Reality / Actuality

**Definition.** This dimension covers the evaluation of whether something actually exists, occurs, or is the case, as opposed to being imagined, fictional, theoretical, or merely apparent. Terms in this dimension are used when the question is not whether a statement is true but whether a referent or situation is real. The contrast is between actual existence and non-existence, appearance, or fiction.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: namdvili (real, genuine, actual), namdviloba (reality, genuineness), sinarmdvile (reality)
- Yoruba: gidi (genuine, real, authentic), jẹ́jẹ́ (genuine, veritable), pàtàkì (genuine, authentic)
- Finnish: todellinen (real, actual), todellisuus (reality), todella (really, truly), tosielämä (real life)
- Basque: benetako (real, genuine), erreala (real), errealitatea (reality), itxurazko (apparent, seeming)
- Tamil: silje (reality, actuality), silche (substance, entity), uṇmainilai (true state, actual situation)
- Indonesian: nyata (real, actual), kenyataan (reality, fact), ternyata (it turns out, evidently)
- Turkish: gerçek (real, genuine), gerçeklik (reality), gerçekten (really, truly), gerçek dışı (unreal)
- Korean: silje (reality, actuality), silche (substance, entity), jinjja (real, genuine), sasil (fact, reality)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. In most languages this dimension is partially distinct from Dimension A (propositional correspondence), though the boundary is not always sharp. Finnish maintains the clearest separation (tosi for propositional truth, todellinen for ontological reality). Turkish gerçek and Korean jinsil/sasil span both dimensions. The dimension consistently generates a contrast between what is real and what is apparent, imagined, or fictional.

---

### DIMENSION D: Material Authenticity / Genuineness of Objects

**Definition.** This dimension covers the evaluation of whether physical objects, documents, goods, or representations are genuine originals as opposed to counterfeits, forgeries, or imitations. Terms in this dimension are used primarily in commercial, legal, and authentication contexts where the question is whether an item is what it purports to be. The focus is on physical or documentary authenticity rather than propositional truth or personal honesty.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: namdvili (genuine, authentic), q'albi (fake, counterfeit), gaq'albeba (falsification, forgery)
- Yoruba: gidi (genuine, real), kì í ṣe gidi (not genuine, not real)
- Finnish: aito (genuine, authentic), aitous (genuineness), väärennös (forgery, counterfeit), väärentää (to forge)
- Basque: egiazko dokumentua (authentic document), gezurrezko dokumentua (false document), faltsua (false, fake), faltsutu (to falsify)
- Tamil: acal (original, genuine), poyp poruḷ (fake object), uṇmaip poruḷ (genuine object), poyeḻuttu (forged document)
- Indonesian: asli (genuine, original), palsu (fake, counterfeit), keaslian (authenticity), pemalsuan (forgery)
- Turkish: asıl (original, genuine), sahte (fake, counterfeit), özgün (original, authentic), sahtekâr (forger)
- Korean: jinpum (genuine article), jinbon (authentic copy), wijo (forgery), gajja (fake, counterfeit)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. In most languages this dimension has dedicated vocabulary distinct from propositional truth terms, though the same adjectives sometimes cover both (Georgian namdvili, Tamil uṇmaiyāna, Turkish gerçek). The dimension consistently generates a genuine/counterfeit opposition and vocabulary for forgery as a legal category. Finnish and Indonesian show the clearest separation from Dimension A.

---

### DIMENSION E: Factual Correctness / Error in Statements or Actions

**Definition.** This dimension covers the evaluation of whether statements, answers, calculations, or actions are correct or incorrect according to established standards, rules, or norms. Terms in this dimension are used in educational, procedural, and evaluative contexts where correctness is determined by conformity to a standard rather than by correspondence to an independently existing state of affairs. The dimension overlaps with Dimension A but is distinguishable by its focus on conformity to criteria rather than correspondence to facts.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: sc'ori (correct, right, straight), mcdari (erroneous, mistaken), gaasc'oreba (correction)
- Yoruba: tọ́ (to be correct), àṣìṣe (error, mistake), ṣe déédé (to do correctly), déédé (correctly, exactly)
- Finnish: oikea (right, correct), väärä (wrong, incorrect), virhe (error, mistake), oikein (correctly)
- Basque: zuzena (correct, right), okerra (wrong, incorrect), zuzendu (to correct), zuzenketa (correction)
- Tamil: cari (correct, right), tappu (mistake, wrong), tavaṟu (mistake, error), cariyāna (correct)
- Indonesian: benar (correct, right), salah (wrong, mistaken), kesalahan (mistake, error), betul (correct)
- Turkish: doğru (correct, right), yanlış (wrong, incorrect), hata (error, mistake), düzeltmek (to correct)
- Korean: matda (to be correct), teullida (to be wrong), teullimeobsi (certainly, without mistake)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. In most languages the same terms cover both Dimension A (propositional correspondence) and this dimension, but Tamil shows the clearest separation (cari/tappu for everyday correctness vs. uṇmai/poy for truth/falsehood). The dimension consistently generates correction vocabulary and is associated with educational and procedural contexts.

---

### DIMENSION F: Reliability / Trustworthiness of Sources

**Definition.** This dimension covers the evaluation of whether persons, sources, or information can be depended upon to provide accurate information consistently over time. Terms in this dimension assess credibility and dependability rather than the truth-value of specific propositions. The focus is on the track record or character of a source rather than on any single statement.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: sando (reliable, trustworthy, credible), sandooba (reliability), uṭq'uari (infallible, unerring)
- Yoruba: fidagarria (reliable, trustworthy), sinesgarria (believable, credible)
- Finnish: luotettava (reliable, trustworthy), luotettavuus (reliability), uskottava (believable, credible)
- Basque: fidagarria (reliable, trustworthy), sinesgarria (believable, credible), zalantzagarria (doubtful)
- Tamil: nampakam (reliability, trustworthiness), sinbingseong (credibility)
- Indonesian: dapat dipercaya (trustworthy), terpercaya (trusted), kredibel (credible)
- Turkish: güvenilir (reliable, trustworthy), güvenilirlik (reliability), inandırıcı (convincing, credible)
- Korean: sinbingseong (credibility, reliability), mideumanada (to be trustworthy), hwaksilhada (to be certain)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages, though the degree of elaboration varies. Basque shows the most elaborate vocabulary for this dimension, with productive -garri suffix creating evaluative adjectives (fidagarria, sinesgarria, zalantzagarria). Finnish also shows high elaboration (luotettava, uskottava, paikkansapitävä). The dimension is consistently distinct from Dimension A: reliability concerns consistent accuracy over time, not the truth of a specific statement.

---

### DIMENSION G: Verification / Authentication Processes

**Definition.** This dimension covers the processes and acts of establishing, confirming, or certifying the truth, accuracy, or authenticity of claims, documents, or identities through investigation, evidence, or formal procedures. Terms in this dimension are used in legal, administrative, scientific, and investigative contexts where truth must be actively established rather than simply asserted.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: damoc'meba (verification, attestation), daadast'ura (confirmed, verified), egiazkotu (to verify)
- Yoruba: ìfẹ̀sẹ̀múlẹ̀ (confirmation, verification), fẹsẹ̀ múlẹ̀ (to confirm, verify), ẹ̀rí (witness, evidence)
- Finnish: todistaa (to prove, testify), todiste (proof, evidence), todentaa (to verify, authenticate), todistustaakka (burden of proof)
- Basque: egiazkotu (to verify, authenticate), egiaztatu (to verify, prove), frogatu (to prove, test), egiaztagiri (certificate)
- Tamil: meyppu (proof, verification), uṇmaippaṭuttu (to verify, authenticate), uṇmaippramāṇam (authoritative proof)
- Indonesian: membenarkan (to confirm, verify), pembenaran (justification, confirmation), memvalidasi (to validate)
- Turkish: doğrulamak (to verify, confirm), doğrulama (verification), kanıtlamak (to prove)
- Korean: sasil hwagin (fact-checking), jinsilgyumyeong (truth clarification), jinwireul garida (to determine authenticity)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. Finnish shows the most elaborate vocabulary for this dimension, with a large family derived from tode- (todistaa, todentaa, todeta, todistus, todistaja, todistustaakka, todistusaineisto). The dimension consistently generates vocabulary for evidence, proof, witnesses, and formal certification. All languages show a gap: no productive causative construction for "making X true" is attested; verification constructions establish that something is true rather than causing it to be true.

---

### DIMENSION H: Revelation / Concealment of Truth

**Definition.** This dimension covers the processes of making hidden truth visible or keeping known truth hidden. Terms in this dimension describe the dynamics of truth disclosure and concealment, focusing on the transition between hidden and known states. The dimension is consistently expressed through constructional pairs (reveal vs. conceal) rather than through dedicated lexical items.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: gamovlinda (was revealed), gamoač'ina (revealed), damala (hid), dap'ara (covered)
- Yoruba: fi òtítọ́ hàn (to show/reveal truth), ṣe àṣírí (to keep secret), irọ́ jáde (lie comes to light)
- Finnish: paljastaa totuus (reveal truth), salata totuus (conceal truth), totuus paljastui (truth was revealed)
- Basque: egia atera (bring out truth), egia ezkutatu (hide truth), gezurra atera (expose a lie)
- Tamil: uṇmai veḷippaṭu (truth comes out), uṇmaiyai maṟai (hide truth), uṇmaiyai veḷippaṭuttu (reveal truth)
- Indonesian: mengungkap kebenaran (reveal truth), menyembunyikan kebenaran (hide truth), ternyata (it turns out)
- Turkish: gerçeği ortaya çıkarmak (bring truth to light), gerçeği gizlemek (hide truth), gerçek ortaya çıkmak (truth comes out)
- Korean: jinsireul balkhida (reveal truth), jinsireul sumgida (hide truth), jinsiri balkhyeojida (truth is revealed)

**Distribution:** Clearly attested in all eight languages, primarily through constructional pairs rather than dedicated lexical items. The dimension is consistently expressed through light verb constructions combining a truth noun with opposing verbs of disclosure and concealment. The intransitive revelation construction (truth reveals itself) is attested in all languages alongside the transitive causative (agent reveals truth). This dimension is closely related to Dimension G (verification) but distinct: verification establishes truth through evidence, while revelation makes hidden truth visible.
